title: When Should You Modify a Parenting Plan in Colorado?

content.rendered:
When your case ended, your parenting plan fit your family’s life at that time. But families don’t stand still. Children grow up, and parents change jobs, remarry, or move. A schedule that worked well for a kindergartner may no longer work for a high schooler with a part-time job, a travel soccer team, and a social calendar busier than yours.

The good news? Your parenting plan isn’t carved in stone. Colorado law expects families to change, and if your current plan no longer fits your children’s lives, you may be able to modify your parenting plan. Here’s how to tell when it’s time, what the court will look for, and what to do first.

Signs It May Be Time to Modify Your Parenting Plan

There’s no single event that triggers a modification, but these are some of the most common reasons parents walk through our door:

  • Your child’s needs have changed. A new school, a medical or mental health diagnosis, special education needs, or simply growing older can make the current schedule a poor fit.
  • A parent is relocating. A move across town can make school-day exchanges impossible. A move out of state almost always requires a new plan.
  • Work schedules have changed. A new shift, frequent travel, or a remote job can affect which parent is actually available during their parenting time.
  • The current schedule isn’t being followed. If one parent regularly skips parenting time, or you’ve both been quietly doing something different for months, the order may no longer reflect real life.
  • There are safety concerns. Substance abuse, domestic violence, neglect, or an unsafe household are serious issues that may justify restricting parenting time.
  • Your teenager has strong, reasoned preferences. (Teenagers with opinions? Shocking, we know.) A mature child’s wishes are one factor the court considers, though they never decide the case on their own, and courts often won’t do much with them.

If you recognize your family in one of these situations, it’s worth taking a fresh look at your plan. Our mid-year parenting plan check-in walks through a simple review.

What Does It Take to Change Your Parenting Plan?

If you’re wondering whether a judge will sign off on a new schedule, the answer depends mostly on one question: how big is the change you’re asking for? Colorado law (C.R.S. § 14-10-129) treats a small tweak and a major overhaul very differently.

Small adjustments that fit your family’s life today

Maybe 5 p.m. exchanges stopped working the day you started your new job. Maybe the holiday rotation has turned every Thanksgiving into a negotiation. Or maybe you’d just like a midweek dinner with your child. If the change doesn’t affect which parent your child lives with most of the time, the court only needs to see that the new schedule is better for your child.

The judge looks at the same things you probably think about every day, using the factors Colorado courts use to decide a child’s best interests: your child’s bond with each parent, how they’re doing at home, at school, and in the community, and whether each parent supports the child’s relationship with the other parent.

Bigger changes, like where your child lives most of the time

If you’re asking for a major shift in parenting time that would also change which home is your child’s main home, the bar is higher. Kids do best with stability, and courts don’t want them bouncing between houses like a ping-pong ball without a good reason. You’ll need to show that something important has changed since the last order (or that the court didn’t know key facts back then), and that the change is truly needed for your child’s well-being.

In practice, courts usually keep the current arrangement unless, for example:

  • You and the other parent both agree to the change;
  • Your child has already become part of your household, with the other parent’s consent;
  • The parent your child lives with most of the time is moving; or
  • Your child’s current home puts their physical health at risk or is seriously harming their emotional development, and a change would do more good than harm.

Already asked once? The two-year wait

Courts don’t love reruns. If a request to change your child’s primary home has already been filed and decided, another request of that kind generally can’t be filed for two years. That wait doesn’t apply if your child’s physical safety or emotional development may be at risk, or if the parent your child lives with most of the time plans to relocate.

The schedule and the big decisions are two different things

Which days your child spends with each parent (parenting time) is separate from who makes the major calls about school, health care, and religion (decision-making responsibility). If your frustration is really about those decisions, changing them also requires showing that circumstances have changed and that the change is needed for your child’s best interests (C.R.S. § 14-10-131).

What If a Parent Wants to Move?

A new job, a new marriage, or the chance to live closer to Grandma can make a move feel like the obvious next step. For the other parent, though, it can turn their relationship with your child upside down. That’s why Colorado has rules for it.

If the parent your child lives with most of the time wants to move with the child far enough to substantially change the child’s connection to the other parent, they must give the other parent written notice as soon as practicable. The notice has to say where they plan to live, why they’re moving, and how parenting time could work after the move. The court then looks at specific relocation factors along with your child’s best interests, and these hearings get priority on the court’s calendar. Learn more in our guide to parental relocation laws in Colorado.

Can Parents Just Agree to Change the Schedule?

Yes, and when you and your co-parent can agree, it’s often the easiest path for everyone, especially your kids. But here’s the catch many parents don’t see coming: an informal agreement, even one in an email or a text thread, doesn’t change your court order. If things fall apart months later, the court will enforce the last order on file, not the arrangement you’ve been following. “But we agreed by text” is not a winning legal argument.

If the new schedule is meant to last, protect it. Put it in a written agreement (called a stipulation) and ask the court to approve it. That way, the new schedule can be enforced and everyone knows the rules.

What If My Child Is in Danger?

If you’re worried your child is in immediate physical or emotional danger during time with the other parent, you don’t have to wait through the regular modification process. You can ask the court to restrict that parent’s time. When the request says the danger is imminent, the court must hear it and decide within 14 days, and any parenting time until then must be supervised (C.R.S. § 14-10-129(4)). Read more about how to apply for emergency custody in Colorado. If a child is in immediate danger, call 911 first.

What to Expect When You Ask for a Change

Every family is different, but most parenting plan changes follow the same basic path:

  1. Start with what your order says now. Before you propose anything, re-read your parenting plan and decision-making orders. You’d be surprised how many parents are fighting about a rule that isn’t actually in there.
  2. Try to work it out together. A direct conversation or a mediator can often settle things faster, for less money, and with a lot less stress on your kids (and your blood pressure). Plus, almost every court requires mediation first before they will consider setting a hearing.  And hey, your parenting plan may require mediation first (check it!)
  3. File a motion if you can’t agree. You’ll explain to the court what has changed and why a new plan is better for your child, usually with a proposed parenting plan.
  4. Go to mediation. Colorado courts typically require parents to try mediation before a contested hearing on modification.
  5. Have your case heard. If mediation doesn’t resolve it, a judge or magistrate will decide at a hearing based on the evidence.

And start keeping records now. School reports, calendars, messages with your co-parent, and anything else that shows how the current plan is (or isn’t) working for your child can make a real difference. Your memory is good; a calendar is better.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long after a parenting plan is entered can I ask to modify it in Colorado?

There’s no general waiting period for asking the court to modify parenting time. However, if a prior motion sought to substantially change parenting time and change the child’s primary residence, a similar motion generally can’t be filed for two years after that motion was decided, unless an exception applies, such as danger to the child or a relocation.

Does my child get to decide where they live?

No. Colorado courts consider a child’s wishes only if the child is mature enough to express reasoned and independent preferences, and those wishes are just one of many best-interest factors. Children are rarely asked to testify. Marie, for example, has never seen a court allow testimony by a child, even a teenager.

Do I need to go to court if my ex and I agree on a new schedule?

To make the change enforceable, the agreement should be submitted to the court for approval. An informal agreement doesn’t change the existing order, and the court will enforce the last order on file if a dispute comes up.

What counts as a change in circumstances?

It depends on the facts, but common examples include a parent relocating, significant changes in a parent’s work schedule, a child’s changing educational, medical, or emotional needs, or concerns about the child’s safety.

Will modifying parenting time change child support?

It can. Child support in Colorado is calculated partly based on the number of overnights each parent has, so a significant change in parenting time may justify a child support modification as well.

Learn more about modifying child support in Colorado.
